passage: Jasleen, puttar, come and sit. I'll tell you about the week my father died. I'm Gurpreet, your Dadi, and I was twenty then. The house filled with relatives. They brought dal and rotis and pickle, and nobody knew what to say, so mostly they said nothing. At first I kept smiling and carrying tea, because I didn't want anyone to feel awkward. Then my Nirmala Chachi came and sat beside me on the floor, shelling peas, quiet as a lamp. Nothing was fixed, nothing could be. But I felt held. That night I told her, "Chachi, please don't go home yet. I don't want to be alone in this room." She stayed until morning. After that I stopped playing host, and people stopped guessing what I needed, because I told them.

qa.q: What was Nirmala Chachi doing while she sat beside Gurpreet?
qa.a: She was shelling peas.

qa.q: How did Gurpreet feel once Nirmala Chachi sat beside her?
qa.a: Held, even though nothing was fixed and nothing could be.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet do that made the visits easier to bear?
qa.a: She stopped playing host and told people what she needed, such as asking Chachi to stay through the night.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Chachi have felt when Gurpreet asked her to stay?
qa.a: Probably glad to be told how to help, since sitting quietly was already her way of offering care.

grounding: Relatives cook, visit and sit quietly after a death; the protagonist feels held though nothing fixes it, and learns to say what she needs.

passage: The power cut left the whole lane dark, and the rain drummed on the tin roof. Jahnavi sat cross-legged in front of the small shrine in her room, a single candle lit. Two weeks ago Rafiq, her friend since Class Six, had died. "Why did you take him?" she said aloud. Then louder, her voice cracking: "He was twenty-one! Why?" Nothing answered but rain. She pressed her hand over her mouth, hot with shame. How could she shout at God? In the morning she carried her tea to Ammamma's room and said it all in one breath. Ammamma didn't hurry her. "Beta, He can bear your questions. Ask them. Anger and faith have sat together in many old hearts." Jahnavi let herself cry, and the question stayed.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do in front of the shrine during the power cut?
qa.a: She sat cross-legged with a single candle lit and asked why Rafiq was taken.

qa.q: Why did Jahnavi feel shame after she shouted?
qa.a: She felt hot with shame because she thought she should not shout at God.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi after that night?
qa.a: Telling Ammamma everything and being allowed to keep asking her questions rather than being pushed to accept.

qa.q: How might Ammamma see Jahnavi's anger?
qa.a: As something that can sit beside faith, not a betrayal of it, since Ammamma says many old hearts hold both.

grounding: The protagonist, angry with God after a friend's death and ashamed of it, is allowed her questions by a patient elder.

passage: Two months after my father died, my mother handed me a folder of papers and said, "You decide, beta, you're the man of the house now." I'm Deepika, and I'm a woman of twenty, so that sentence landed strangely. I was proud that she trusted me. I was also so heavy that I couldn't lift my arms some evenings. I sat with those papers at midnight and realised I hadn't cried for Papa once, because I was too busy being useful. So I rang my Kishore Mama and asked him to come. He sat with Mummy, and some cousins took over the small daily jobs. Mummy still leans on me, and I still hold her. But I've let myself grieve too, out loud, in the balcony at night.

qa.q: What did Deepika's mother hand her two months after her father died?
qa.a: She handed Deepika a folder of papers.

qa.q: Why did Deepika feel both proud and heavy?
qa.a: She was proud that her mother trusted her, but heavy because she was doing everything and had not cried for Papa.

qa.q: What did Deepika do to stop carrying everything alone?
qa.a: She called Kishore Mama to come, let cousins take over small daily jobs, and let herself grieve too.

qa.q: How might Deepika's mother see the folder handover?
qa.a: She may see it as trust and a way of coping with her own loss, without noticing how heavy it is for Deepika.

grounding: After the father's death the mother leans on the protagonist as if she were the adult; she feels pride and heaviness and shares the load with relatives.

passage: Arjun, your Mama is going to tell you something I never told anyone. I'm Vijay. One week after my father's funeral, I sat at the tea stall and felt nothing. Not sadness, not anger, nothing. Everyone expected tears. I thought, what is wrong with me? I even copied the relatives, making my face long. My Masi Sarita found me on the steps that evening. "Beta, when the heart gets too full, sometimes it goes quiet to protect you. Don't argue with yourself." She made me keep small routines: tea at six, a walk, dinner with everyone. "And if it stays quiet a long time, we will see a doctor," she said. It lifted after some weeks. I cried at an odd moment, over a lost slipper, and Masi just handed me water.

qa.q: Where was Vijay sitting when he felt nothing a week after the funeral?
qa.a: Vijay was at the tea stall.

qa.q: What was Vijay worried about?
qa.a: That something was wrong with him because he felt nothing while everyone expected tears.

qa.q: What helped Vijay through the numbness?
qa.a: Keeping small routines such as tea, a walk and dinner with everyone, and Masi Sarita's patience, with a doctor as a plan if it stayed.

qa.q: How might Masi Sarita see Vijay's numbness?
qa.a: As the heart going quiet to protect him, not a sign that he did not love his father.

grounding: A week after the funeral the protagonist feels nothing and worries; an elder relative calls numbness a protection and advises patience, routine and help if it persists.

passage:
"Joseph, you've barely touched your food," said Reena, setting her tray down.
"Everyone's talking about the fest." He stirred his rice. "Nobody's asked about Ajji. She died three weeks ago."
"I didn't know if I should bring it up."
"It's like the whole class pressed play and I'm still on pause. I thought nobody cared."
"I do care. I just didn't want to hurt you by asking."
Joseph looked up. "It hurts more when nobody asks. Could you ask how I'm doing, sometimes? And sit with me at lunch this week?"
"Yes. Both. And I'll tell Meena and Sam, if you want."
"Please," he said, and it was the first breath that had gone all the way down in days.

qa.q: How long ago had Joseph's grandmother died?
qa.a: She died three weeks ago.

qa.q: What did Joseph feel while the class talked about the fest?
qa.a: Frozen and unseen, as if everyone else had pressed play while he stayed on pause.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that helped, and how?
qa.a: He told Reena plainly what he needed, being asked how he was and having company at lunch.

qa.q: Why might Reena not have asked about Joseph's grandmother earlier?
qa.a: She feared that asking would hurt him, so her silence came from caution rather than not caring.

grounding: Classmates return to normal life while the protagonist feels frozen; naming what he needs to a peer opens support.

passage: Priya, sit. I'm Ayesha, and I was twenty-two and new at the firm when it happened. A coworker heard me on the phone with my mother and started mimicking my accent across the desks, saying, "Oh, so cute, do it again!" People laughed. Heat crawled up my neck and I felt small. I nearly laughed along. Instead I said quietly, "Please don't mimic how I talk. It isn't funny to me." That evening I wrote down the date, the words and who was there. The next day I went to Keerthana, a senior I trusted, and she took it to HR with me. There was a conversation, and the mimicking stopped. What I really learned is that the fault sat in the joke, never in how I speak.

qa.q: How old was Ayesha when the mimicking happened?
qa.a: Ayesha was twenty-two.

qa.q: How did Ayesha feel when the accent was mimicked?
qa.a: Hot with embarrassment and small, and Ayesha nearly laughed along.

qa.q: What steps did Ayesha take that made the response effective?
qa.a: She said calmly that it wasn't funny, wrote down the date, words and witnesses, and went to Keerthana and HR.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have seen Ayesha coming to her?
qa.a: As a sign of trust, and as a chance to help a new colleague take the issue to HR properly.

grounding: A coworker jokes about the protagonist's accent; the protagonist feels heat and shame, names it calmly, notes it and uses a senior and HR.

passage: With the hostel closing in three days and monsoon rain flooding the road, Afreen stood under a shop awning while the broker held out his phone. "Jagdish-ji says no. He won't rent to your community. Sorry." He shrugged as if it were about the weather. Afreen's face burned. She was angry and, underneath, small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself. Then she reminded herself that a refusal like this shows what the landlord believes, not what she is. She opened her notes app and typed the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name. She rang Sana from the college legal aid clinic, who offered to explain her options. That evening Afreen's classmate said her cousin had a room going, and Afreen went to see it in the rain.

qa.q: How many days were left before the hostel closed?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel beneath her anger after the refusal?
qa.a: She felt small, as though she had done something wrong by being herself.

qa.q: What did Afreen do that turned the refusal into action?
qa.a: She noted the date, the broker's words and the landlord's name, contacted the legal aid clinic and followed a lead on another room.

qa.q: How might Jagdish see his refusal?
qa.a: He may see it as an ordinary decision about his property, though it rests on a prejudice that reflects on him, not on Afreen.

grounding: A landlord refuses her because of who she is; she feels angry and small, keeps notes, seeks legal aid and allies, and finds another option.

passage: Tutor's note, Thursday. Yamini's classmates did an imitation of her accent in the corridor today, and one of them, Vaibhav, held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and said, "just banter, yaar." Yamini laughed along, but her eyes went to the floor and she wrapped her tiffin in her bag quickly. At the end of the day I asked her to stay back. She said, "I laugh so they don't think I'm sensitive. But it hurts." I told her the mockery was not hers to carry. She practised a plain sentence with me: "That's not okay with me." Yamini said it to Vaibhav on Friday morning, and he went quiet, then said sorry. I have spoken to the whole class about mimicry. I will check in with her next week.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do at Yamini's lunch?
qa.a: Vaibhav held his nose at her home-cooked lunch and called it just banter.

qa.q: Why did Yamini laugh along with the mimicking?
qa.a: She laughed so people would not think she was sensitive, though it hurt her.

qa.q: What plain sentence helped Yamini respond?
qa.a: She practised the sentence "That's not okay with me" and said it to Vaibhav.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav have seen the mimicry before Yamini spoke up?
qa.a: As harmless banter, since Yamini laughed along, though her reply made him go quiet and apologise.

grounding: Classmates mimic her accent and food and call it banter; she laughs along while hurt, then tells them plainly it is not fine.

passage: I'm Sabina, and this is what I saw in the canteen on Tuesday. A group at the next table started mocking Dorjee, a first-year, about where he comes from, doing a sing-song imitation of his speech. Dorjee went very still. Karthik was sitting two seats from them with his fork in the air. He said nothing. His jaw was tight and he stared at his plate, and he left half his lunch. I can't say exactly what he was feeling. Twenty minutes later I saw Karthik find Dorjee outside the library. I couldn't hear all of it, but I caught, "That wasn't right, and I should have said something." On Thursday, when the same table started up again, Karthik said, "Stop that," before anyone else did.

qa.q: Who was sitting two seats from the group that mocked Dorjee?
qa.a: Karthik was sitting two seats from them.

qa.q: What might Karthik have been feeling while he stared at his plate?
qa.a: Possibly uneasy and guilty, since his jaw was tight, he left half his lunch and later apologised, though Sabina says she cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Karthik do afterwards that helped?
qa.a: He checked on Dorjee outside the library and, on Thursday, spoke up against the mockery himself.

qa.q: How might Dorjee have felt when Karthik came to talk?
qa.a: Possibly relieved to be noticed after going very still, since someone acknowledged that the mockery was wrong.

grounding: A bystander who watched a boy insulted for his background stays silent, feels guilty, then checks on him and backs him up next time.

passage: I'm Imran, and I still remember how my hands shook at the bus stop that Monday. A man behind me muttered something vile about my community, loud enough for the queue to hear. Nobody said a word. Every part of me wanted to turn around and hit him. I could feel the anger climbing, and I'll be honest, it felt justified. Then my friend Parveen took my sleeve. "Your anger is fair. Don't let him decide what you do with it. Come." We walked to the college office. It took three hours of forms and a long talk with the counsellor, and it felt so slow. But I wasn't alone with it, and later I joined the student group that helps people who face this. The rage cooled into something I could use.

qa.q: Where was Imran when the insult happened?
qa.a: Imran was at the bus stop.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling as the man muttered?
qa.a: Anger that felt justified and a strong urge to hit him, along with shaking hands.

qa.q: What did Imran and Parveen do with the anger?
qa.a: They went to the college office to file a complaint and talk to the counsellor, and Imran later joined a student support group.

qa.q: How might Parveen have seen Imran's anger?
qa.a: As fair and understandable, yet something to guide before it turned into a fight that could hurt Imran.

grounding: The protagonist wants to hit back at someone who insulted the community; a friend helps direct the anger into a complaint and support.
